question: Why did re-uploading the same CSV return HTTP 409?
title: Redis SHA-256 Duplicate File Lock (DUP-1 & DUP-2)
tldr: Re-uploading the same file returns HTTP 409 Conflict because the backend calculates the SHA-256 cryptographic digest of incoming file streams and checks Redis for the key file_hash:{hash_hex}. If the key already exists within its 24-hour TTL (86,400 seconds), the upload is immediately rejected to prevent redundant database writes and Celery queue congestion.
body: Under Stage 1 (DUP-1 and DUP-2) of the hardening roadmap, backend/app/routers/ingest.py streams the uploaded multipart file to a temporary file while computing its SHA-256 hash. Before scheduling Celery task process_ingest_file.delay(), it probes Redis (redis.from_url(settings.redis_url)) for file_hash:{hash_hex}. If present, it unlinks the temp file and raises HTTPException(status_code=409, detail={'detail': 'Duplicate upload detected — this file was already ingested.', 'original_task_id': existing_task_id}). If absent, it records file_hash:{hash_hex} in Redis with ex=86400 (24-hour expiration) and stores the task.id. Additionally, if a file has distinct hashes but contains identical txid records, PostgreSQL's primary key unique constraint rejects row insertions, and Celery reports total_inserted == 0 AND total_rejected == total_received, triggering an orange warning banner in IngestModal.tsx.

question: How does the ingestion pipeline achieve 10,000+ rows/second throughput?
title: PostgreSQL Bulk COPY Stream Engine
tldr: The pipeline uses PostgreSQL's native binary COPY protocol rather than row-by-row ORM INSERT statements, streaming validated Pydantic in-memory CSV buffers directly into the transactions table. This achieves verified ingestion speeds of 8.38s–12.04s for 100,000 transactions (8,300–11,900 rows/sec).
body: During the initial architecture audit (Phase 0/2), traditional SQLAlchemy ORM inserts bottlenecked at ~250 rows/sec due to round-trip query serialization and transaction boundaries. In Phase 2, backend/app/tasks/ingest.py was re-engineered to employ psycopg2/psycopg3's copy_expert / copy_records_to_table. Transactions are parsed from CSV, JSON, or XML, validated through Pydantic models, enriched with MaxMind GeoIP metadata, and formatted into an in-memory io.StringIO TSV buffer. This buffer is pushed to PostgreSQL via COPY transactions FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT csv, NULL '\N', QUOTE '"', ESCAPE '"'), achieving 100,000 rows in 8.38s–12.04s with verified zero data loss.

question: How are IP addresses enriched with Country and ASN offline without internet access?
title: MaxMind GeoLite2 Binary MMDB Offline Resolution
tldr: Network telemetry is resolved entirely offline via local MaxMind binary databases (GeoLite2-City.mmdb and GeoLite2-ASN.mmdb) mounted directly in the container or backend data directory. Zero external HTTP/DNS lookups occur at runtime, ensuring strict sovereign air-gap isolation.
body: In compliance with national security intelligence air-gap standards, all IP enrichment operates locally using maxminddb memory-mapped reader objects. At worker boot, GeoLite2-City.mmdb and GeoLite2-ASN.mmdb are opened from data/geoip/. For every transaction record, the source IP (src_ip) and destination IP (dst_ip) are queried against the local radix tree in under 5 microseconds per lookup. Country ISO codes, city names, autonomous system numbers (ASNs), and organization names are populated into geo_country and asn columns before the bulk COPY write, achieving 100% enrichment across all 100,000 benchmark records.

question: How does the ingest system handle disparate CSV, JSON, and XML formats?

question: What is the graph database schema and how are entity relationships defined?
title: Neo4j Property Graph Topology (:Wallet, :Transaction, :IP)
tldr: The graph schema mirrors transactional flow using three primary node labels (:Wallet, :Transaction, :IP) interconnected by :SENDS, :RECEIVES, :OBSERVED, and :CO_SPEND relationships, creating a queryable multi-relational forensic topology.
body: PostgreSQL transaction rows are projected into Neo4j using parameterized UNWIND MERGE batches. Node types include :Wallet (uniquely indexed by address string, holding cluster_id, risk_score, and seed_proximity), :Transaction (uniquely indexed by txid, holding block_height, fee, is_mixing, and chain_hops), and :IP (indexed by ipv4 string). Edges represent directional blockchain flow: (:Wallet)-[:SENDS]->(:Transaction) for inputs, (:Transaction)-[:RECEIVES]->(:Wallet) for outputs, (:IP)-[:OBSERVED]->(:Transaction) for network observations, and (:Wallet)-[:CO_SPEND]->(:Wallet) connecting wallets co-spending in the same multi-input transaction.

question: How does Neo4j GDS Louvain modularity group Bitcoin wallets into entity clusters?
title: Neo4j GDS Louvain Entity Clustering (Modularity Q=0.4613)
tldr: Neo4j Graph Data Science (GDS) Louvain community detection executes on the projected :CO_SPEND wallet subgraph, optimizing modularity to Q=0.461314 across 5 hierarchical levels. It identified 9,794 distinct wallet communities, with the largest entity cluster comprising 1,751 wallets.
body: Under the Common Input Ownership Heuristic (CIOH), multiple addresses providing inputs to the same Bitcoin transaction are controlled by the same legal entity. In Phase 4, gds.graph.project extracts the undirected :CO_SPEND wallet graph into an in-memory graph catalog. gds.louvain.write iteratively optimizes modularity Q = (1 / 2m) * sum(A_vw - (k_v * k_w / 2m)). The algorithm converged at Q = 0.461314 across 5 levels, assigning a persistent cluster_id integer to all 24,673 wallets. These IDs are synchronized back to PostgreSQL (UPDATE transactions t SET cluster_id = ...) in 3.43s, establishing entity boundaries for downstream ML feature engineering.

question: Why is the Cypher condition w1.address < w2.address critical in graph queries?
title: Canonical Lexicographic Directional Optimization (w1 < w2)
tldr: The w1.address < w2.address predicate prevents bidirectional reciprocal limit burning and query timeouts during Neo4j traversals by enforcing a single canonical ordering for undirected :CO_SPEND relationships.
body: In an undirected co-spend graph, if wallet A and wallet B co-spend, Cypher pattern (w1:Wallet)-[:CO_SPEND]-(w2:Wallet) matches both (A, B) and (B, A). When generating subgraphs or extracting bounded neighborhoods in backend/app/routers/graph.py, evaluating both permutations doubles the traversal depth, burns through the max_nodes=150 query budget prematurely, and causes memory exhaustion on dense clusters. In Phase 9.5 hardening, adding WHERE w1.address < w2.address and maintaining a bi-directional deduplication set seen_links.add(tuple(sorted([w1, w2]))) slashed traversal latency by 52% and completely eliminated Neo4j query timeouts.

question: How does Personalized PageRank propagate illicit risk from Ransomwhere seed addresses?
title: GDS Personalized PageRank (PPR) Seed Proximity Scoring
tldr: Personalized PageRank initiates random walks biased toward 11,186 verified Ransomwhere seed addresses (damping factor γ=0.85, 20 iterations), computing a continuous topological proximity score (seed_proximity) across 17,474 connected wallets.
body: Ransomware operators routinely launder funds through intermediary hops to distance outputs from law-enforcement blacklists. In Phase 7 and Phase 9.5, Neo4j GDS runs Personalized PageRank on the projected transaction-wallet graph using sourceNodes: seed_node_ids, dampingFactor: 0.85, and maxIterations: 20. The walk probability distribution concentrates mass on addresses structurally proximate to illicit nodes. The resulting seed_proximity floating-point value was persisted to Neo4j via write_pagerank_to_neo4j() and stored in evidence_trails.json across 12,750 wallets with non-zero proximity, serving as a high-value topological feature for GraphSAGE and the Relational Graph Transformer.

question: How does peeling chain traversal work in Cypher?
title: Peeling-Chain Cypher Traversal (>=5 Hops & 97.2% Recall)
tldr: Peeling chains are detected via parameterized Cypher traversals identifying consecutive linear 1-input 2-output transactions where one output peels off a small payment (<=5%) while the remainder (>=80%) forwards as change for at least 5 consecutive hops. The engine achieved 97.2% recall on injected chains.
body: A peeling chain is a money-laundering technique where a large balance is incrementally peeled into small payments across dozens of intermediate addresses. backend/scripts/detect_peeling_chains.py executes a multi-hop Cypher traversal: MATCH path = (t1:Transaction)-[:RECEIVES]->(w:Wallet)-[:SENDS]->(t2:Transaction)... The query filters for input_count == 1 AND output_count == 2, verifies the change output carries >= 80% of input value while the peel output is <= 5%, and enforces chain length >= 5 hops. Across 100,000 synthetic transactions, it scanned 3,207 candidates, qualified 133 distinct chains, and flagged 616 transactions with is_mixing=true and chain_hops >= 5, attaining 97.2% recall (451/464 injected peeling transactions) in 87.1s.

question: How does the system identify CoinJoin mixing transactions?
title: CoinJoin Multi-Party Heuristic (100% Recall)
tldr: CoinJoin mixers are identified through structural heuristic criteria: >=3 distinct inputs, >=3 distinct outputs, equal-value output amounts within +/-1% variance, and a minimum volume threshold of >=0.05 BTC. The algorithm achieved 100.0% recall on synthetic mixing pools.
body: CoinJoin protocols (such as Wasabi, Samourai Whirlpool, and JoinMarket) obfuscate transaction history by combining inputs from multiple independent participants into a single multi-party transaction with uniform output denominations. In Phase 6, backend/scripts/detect_coinjoin.py queries PostgreSQL and Neo4j for transactions satisfying: array_length(input_addresses, 1) >= 3, array_length(output_amounts, 1) >= 3, standard deviation of the top-N outputs <= 0.01 * mean, and output amounts >= 0.05 BTC. The detector inspected 593 structural candidates, qualified 67 true CoinJoin clusters, and attained 100.0% recall (50/50 injected patterns) with zero false negatives in under 0.96s.

question: How does FT-Transformer compute anomaly scores?
title: FT-Transformer (Feature Tokenizer Transformer) Architecture
tldr: FT-Transformer projects 18 continuous tabular features into 32-dimensional embedding tokens, prepends a learnable [CLS] token, processes them through 2 multi-head self-attention layers (4 heads, d_ff=64), and reconstructs the normalized vector from [CLS]. Anomaly score is computed as normalized Mean Squared Error (MSE).
body: Implemented in backend/app/ml/ft_transformer.py, FT-Transformer supersedes traditional MLP autoencoders by explicitly modeling cross-feature non-linear interactions. Each feature x_i is tokenized via linear projection e_i = x_i * W_i + b_i in R^32. The sequence E = [e_cls, e_1, ..., e_18] in R^(19x32) passes through 2 Transformer Encoder blocks with Multi-Head Self-Attention: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q*K^T / sqrt(d_k))*V. A linear head on the final [CLS] token projects back to reconstruct normalized tensor X_hat in R^18. The anomaly score is the normalized reconstruction MSE: L_MSE = (1/18) * sum((x_i - x_hat_i)^2). The model exports an 18x18 self-attention matrix A_(1:,1:) visualizing pairwise feature importance.

question: What is the Composite Risk Formula and how are risk tiers determined?
title: Multi-Factor Composite Risk Scoring Formula & Verdict Tiers
tldr: The composite risk score combines four orthogonal forensic dimensions: score = clip(0.35 * anomaly + 0.45 * risk + 0.15 * rule_bonus + 0.05 * mixing, 0, 1). Scores map to four verdict tiers: CRITICAL (>=0.80), HIGH (0.60–0.80), MEDIUM (0.40–0.60), and LOW (<0.40).
body: In Phase 8, backend/scripts/compute_composite_risk.py fused tabular anomaly detection, graph neural network risk propagation, and deterministic heuristic detections into a calibrated score: Score = min(1.0, max(0.0, 0.35 * anomaly + 0.45 * risk + 0.15 * rule_bonus + 0.05 * mixing)). Here, rule_bonus = min(len(triggered_rules), 5) / 5.0 (each AML rule hit contributes 0.20 up to 5 rules, capped at 1.0), and mixing is a binary 1.0/0.0 flag. Verdict tiers are categorized as CRITICAL (>=0.80), HIGH (0.60–0.80), MEDIUM (0.40–0.60), and LOW (<0.40). Across 17,020 indexed wallets, distribution resulted in: CRITICAL = 103 (0.6%, all with non-empty triggered rules), HIGH = 78 (0.5%), MEDIUM = 3,377 (19.8%), and LOW = 13,462 (79.1%).

question: How does SHAP explain why a transaction is flagged as anomalous?

question: How does GNNExplainer extract topological evidence subgraphs?

question: Why Celery does not write directly to xai_store in Phase 11?
title: Process Isolation Boundary Between Celery and FastAPI
tldr: Celery workers run in a completely isolated OS process with independent virtual memory space and zero shared memory with the FastAPI Uvicorn master process. Celery cannot mutate FastAPI's in-memory xai_store dictionaries directly.
body: A fundamental distributed systems pitfall is attempting to share in-memory state across process boundaries. xai_store.py resides inside the FastAPI web server process memory to deliver sub-millisecond /entity/{address}/explain lookups. Celery executes in a separate Python process (celery worker), connected to FastAPI only via Redis and PostgreSQL. Any dictionary mutation performed inside a Celery task alters only that worker's private copy and vanishes upon task exit. To solve this in Phase 11, the architecture uses a two-phase protocol: Celery handles bulk parsing, GeoIP enrichment, and Postgres insertion; upon Celery SUCCESS, the frontend triggers POST /ingest/sync/{task_id} inside FastAPI, which executes inline scoring and mutates the live xai_store.

question: How does the POST /ingest/sync/{task_id} endpoint work?
title: POST /ingest/sync/{task_id} Endpoint Architecture & Workflow
tldr: POST /ingest/sync/{task_id} executes inside the FastAPI process, queries PostgreSQL for transactions ingested within the past 2 minutes, runs inline_scorer.score_batch() to compute Autoencoder/FT-Transformer MSE and rule checks, and atomically upserts results into xai_store.
body: Under Stage 2 (Phase 11.3), backend/app/routers/ingest.py exposes POST /ingest/sync/{task_id}. When invoked, it: 1) Checks Redis for sync_done:{task_id} to enforce idempotency (returning 409 if already synced), 2) Queries PostgreSQL: SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE ingested_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '2 minutes', 3) Passes rows to inline_scorer.score_batch(), which extracts 18 features, runs CPU model inference, and checks for Ransomwhere seed overlap or peeling candidates, 4) Calls xai_store.upsert_composite() and upsert_evidence() using threading.RLock, and 5) Sets sync_done:{task_id} in Redis with a 3,600s TTL. It returns HTTP 200 with { 'scored': N, 'upserted': N, 'skipped_existing': N }.

question: How does xai_store prevent race conditions during live mutation?
title: Thread-Safe In-Memory Store Mutation with threading.RLock
tldr: xai_store.py uses a re-entrant lock (threading.RLock()) wrapping upsert_composite, upsert_evidence, and atomic upsert_batch functions, preventing dictionary mutation race conditions between concurrent sync operations and analytical read requests.
body: FastAPI runs under Uvicorn with an asynchronous event loop and a thread pool executor for synchronous endpoint defs. If an analyst requests GET /entity/{addr}/explain on thread A while POST /ingest/sync/{task_id} executes batch upserts on thread B, simultaneous dictionary modification in Python can cause RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration or return partially written records. Under Phase 11.1, backend/app/services/xai_store.py introduced _store_lock = threading.RLock(). All mutations (upsert_composite, upsert_evidence, upsert_batch) and atomic bulk lookups acquire _store_lock, ensuring strict thread-safety while preserving sub-millisecond read access.

question: What are the local development server ports and their allocated services?
title: System Port Allocation & Infrastructure Mappings
tldr: The sovereign platform uses 6 standard local ports: 8000 (FastAPI Backend), 3000 (Next.js Command Center), 3001 (RAG Technical Documentation), 5432 (PostgreSQL), 7687 (Neo4j Bolt) / 7474 (Neo4j HTTP), and 6379 (Redis).
body: Per dev-server.md, running the full stack bare-metal without Docker relies on pre-allocated ports: 1) Port 8000: FastAPI backend REST API (uvicorn app.main:app), 2) Port 3000: Next.js forensic analyst surveillance dashboard (frontend), 3) Port 3001: Next.js RAG technical documentation portal (rag), 4) Port 5432: PostgreSQL relational transaction database (sih_bitcoin), 5) Port 7687: Neo4j Bolt graph protocol (with Port 7474 for Neo4j Web Browser UI), 6) Port 6379: Redis in-memory cache, Celery message broker, and idempotency lock.

question: How do I run backend and celery locally without Docker?
title: Three-Terminal Bare-Metal Startup Runbook (dev-server.md)
tldr: Start the platform locally by opening 3 terminals: Terminal 1 runs alembic upgrade head and uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000; Terminal 2 runs celery -A app.celery_app worker --loglevel=info --pool=solo; Terminal 3 runs npm run dev on port 3000.
body: As specified in dev-server.md, three separate terminal windows are required: Terminal 1 (FastAPI Backend): cd backend; .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1; alembic upgrade head; uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000. Terminal 2 (Celery Ingest Worker): cd backend; .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1; celery -A app.celery_app worker --loglevel=info --pool=solo. Terminal 3 (Next.js Dashboard): cd frontend; npm install; npm run dev. To verify pipeline health: curl http://localhost:8000/health (returns healthy status for database, neo4j, and redis).

question: Why must Celery be executed with --pool=solo on Windows?
title: Windows Multiprocessing Constraints & Celery --pool=solo
tldr: Windows does not support the POSIX fork() system call. Running Celery without --pool=solo causes worker processes to deadlock, freeze silently during task dispatch, or trigger WinError 10061 permission errors.
body: By default, Celery spawns child worker processes using POSIX fork(), which duplicates parent process memory space on Linux/macOS. On Windows, Python falls back to spawn, which re-imports the entire application module tree in each subprocess. This causes circular import deadlocks, unpicklable object errors, and permission failures when binding to Redis on Windows. Adding --pool=solo forces Celery to execute tasks inline within a single dedicated worker thread, eliminating multiprocessing race conditions and guaranteeing reliable async ingestion on Windows host environments.

question: What is AddressHashMiddleware and why are Bitcoin addresses masked in logs?
title: AddressHashMiddleware Log Anonymization & Privacy Guard
tldr: AddressHashMiddleware intercepts incoming HTTP requests and outgoing responses, replacing all Base58 and Bech32 Bitcoin wallet strings with SHA-256 token digests in console and disk logs to prevent plaintext wallet intelligence leaks.
body: In compliance with intelligence operational security protocols, surveillance analysts must not expose sensitive wallet addresses in application log aggregators (e.g. Datadog, CloudWatch, or local stdout). Address pseudonymization is implemented as a root Python logging filter (_AddressPseudonymFilter) in backend/app/main.py that intercepts all log messages using regex patterns for Bitcoin P2PKH (starts with 1), P2SH (starts with 3), and SegWit/Taproot (starts with bc1). Matched addresses are converted into 8-character SHA256 hex digests ([:8]) formatted as [addr:<hash8>] before passing to the Python standard logging facility, ensuring zero plaintext wallet addresses leak in telemetry logs.

question: How is the entire backend and ML pipeline verified with Pytest?
title: Comprehensive 196-Test Pytest Verification Suite
tldr: The entire backend, ML inference engines, graph heuristics, and Phase 11 sync services are covered by a suite of 196 automated pytest tests (pytest backend/tests/ -v), verifying zero regressions across all system components.
body: The backend test harness in backend/tests/ provides deterministic unit and integration test coverage across all completed phases: Phase 2 ingest parsing & deduplication (test_ingest.py, test_dup_ingest.py), Phase 3/4 Neo4j graph & Louvain clustering (test_graph_build.py, test_phase4_clustering.py), Phase 5/7 Dual Transformer & GraphSAGE inference (test_ft_transformer.py, test_graph_transformer.py, test_phase5_autoencoder.py, test_phase7_graphsage.py), Phase 6 peeling and CoinJoin heuristic detectors (test_phase6_detectors.py, test_feature_extractor.py), Phase 8 XAI stores (test_phase8_xai.py), Phase 9/9.5 API endpoints (test_alerts_endpoint.py, test_graph_router.py, test_entity_subgraph.py), and Phase 11 live sync (test_ingest_sync.py, test_inline_scorer.py). All 196 tests execute in under 45 seconds on CPU with 100% pass rate and zero regressions.
